los.text: Describe the common causes, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms of haematuria
los.html:
• Visible (macroscopic) vs non-visible (dipstick/microscopic, ≥1+ on 2 of 3 tests).
    • Exclude false positives: menstruation, myoglobin, beetroot/rifampicin (red urine, dipstick negative), exercise.
SiteCauses
KidneyGlomerular (IgA nephropathy, post-infectious GN: dysmorphic RBCs, casts, proteinuria, ↑BP); RCC; stones; polycystic kidneys; trauma; papillary necrosis
UreterStones, urothelial carcinoma
BladderUrothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, infection (cystitis), stones, schistosomiasis
Prostate/urethraBPH, prostate cancer, urethritis, trauma, catheter
SystemicAnticoagulation (still investigate), sickle cell, bleeding disorders
  • Symptoms: painless visible haematuria (cancer until proven otherwise)
    • with loin-to-groin colicky pain (stone)
    • with dysuria/frequency (UTI)
    • clots (lower tract bleeding, retention risk).
Painless visible haematuria in an adult = urothelial cancer until proven otherwise.

los.text: Describe the investigations and principles of treatment and management of haematuria
los.html:
Initial testsUrine dipstick, MSU culture, urine ACR/PCR (glomerular), U&E/eGFR, FBC, clotting, PSA (men, after counselling), BP.
2-week-wait urology referral (NICE NG12)
  • Age ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria (without UTI, or persisting after treated UTI)
  • Age ≥60 with non-visible haematuria + dysuria or raised WCC.
Haematuria clinic ("one-stop")Flexible cystoscopy (bladder) + upper tract imaging (CT urogram for visible haematuria; USS for non-visible/younger patients).
Nephrology referral if glomerular features: proteinuria, ↓ eGFR, hypertension, dysmorphic red cells/casts, age <40 with non-visible haematuria.
ManagementTreat cause (antibiotics, stone management, TURBT). Clot retention → 3-way catheter + bladder irrigation. Resuscitate if heavy bleeding; correct coagulopathy.

los.text: Describe the types, pathophysiology, presentations, diagnosis and treatment principles for bladder and upper urinary tract cancer
los.html:
• Urothelial carcinoma (~90% bladder cancers; also renal pelvis/ureter).
  • Risk factors: smoking (biggest), aromatic amines (dye, rubber, leather industries), cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiotherapy.
  • Squamous cell with schistosomiasis and chronic catheter/stones.
  • Adenocarcinoma with urachal remnant.
PresentationPainless visible haematuria; irritative LUTS (carcinoma in situ); upper tract → loin pain, hydronephrosis.
DiagnosisCystoscopy → TURBT (diagnosis + staging: must include detrusor muscle); CT urogram; urine cytology; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging.
Non-muscle-invasive (Ta, T1, CIS; ~75%)TURBT + single intravesical mitomycin C; intermediate/high risk → intravesical BCG; regular surveillance cystoscopy (high recurrence).
Muscle-invasive (≥T2)Neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy + radical cystectomy with ileal conduit or neobladder, or radical radiotherapy (bladder preservation). Metastatic: chemotherapy, immunotherapy.
Upper tract urothelial carcinomaNephroureterectomy (with bladder cuff); ureteroscopy for staging/low-risk lesions. Associated with Lynch syndrome.
Renal cell carcinoma(different, from tubules)Haematuria, loin pain, mass; often incidental on imaging. Rx: partial/radical nephrectomy.

los.text: Describe the investigations and principles of treatment and management of urinary stone disease
sessions: Clin 4: Principles of management of urinary stone disease
los.html:
PresentationSudden severe loin-to-groin colic, restless patient, nausea/vomiting, haematuria. Fever + obstructed kidney = emergency.
Ix
  • Urine dipstick (blood), MSU, U&E, Ca²⁺, urate, FBC/CRP.
  • Non-contrast CT KUB within 24 h (gold standard; USS in pregnancy/children).
  • Stone analysis.
Stone typesCalcium oxalate (~80%), calcium phosphate, urate (radiolucent on X-ray, acidic urine; gout, tumour lysis), struvite (Proteus/urease → staghorn), cystine.
Acute management
  • NSAID analgesia first (IM/PR diclofenac or similar) unless contraindicated, then IV paracetamol/opioids; antiemetic.
  • <5 mm: most pass spontaneously → watchful waiting.
  • 5–10 mm distal ureteric: medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker, tamsulosin).
  • Larger/failed: ureteroscopy (laser), shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL, <2 cm renal), PCNL (large/staghorn renal stones).
Obstructed and infected kidney (fever, sepsis) → urgent decompression: nephrostomy or retrograde JJ stent + IV antibiotics.
  • Prevention: fluids >2.5 L/day, ↓ salt and animal protein, normal calcium intake; potassium citrate (low citrate), thiazides (hypercalciuria), allopurinol (urate).

los.text: Describe the structure and function of the kidneys
los.html:
Gross
  • Retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (right slightly lower due to liver).
  • Capsule → cortex (glomeruli) and medulla (pyramids) → papillae → minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis → ureter.
  • Hilum (anterior → posterior): vein, artery, pelvis.
Blood supply
  • Renal artery
  • → segmental
  • → interlobar
  • → arcuate
  • → interlobular
  • → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole
  • → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons).
  • Kidneys get ~20–25% of cardiac output.
Nephron(~1 million per kidney)
  • Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct.
  • Cortical (85%) and juxtamedullary (long loops; concentrate urine) nephrons.
Juxtaglomerular apparatusMacula densa (senses NaCl in DCT), JG cells (renin), mesangial cells.
Functions("A WET BED")Acid–base, Water balance, Electrolytes, Toxin/waste removal (urea, creatinine, drugs), Blood pressure (RAAS, Na⁺), Erythropoietin, D (1α-hydroxylation → calcitriol). Also gluconeogenesis.

los.text: Explain the processes involved in the formation of urine (filtration, secretion and reabsorption)
los.html:
Filtration(glomerulus)~180 L/day; filtrate = plasma minus proteins/cells. Barrier: fenestrated endothelium, negatively charged glomerular basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms (nephrin).
Reabsorption
  • PCT (~65% of Na⁺ and water): all glucose and amino acids (SGLT2, SGLT1), ~80% HCO₃⁻ (via carbonic anhydrase), phosphate, K⁺, urea (~50%). Iso-osmotic.
  • Loop of Henle: descending limb permeable to water only; thick ascending limb impermeable to water, reabsorbs Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ (NKCC2; loop diuretics) → dilute tubular fluid; creates medullary concentration gradient (countercurrent multiplication; ~25% of Na⁺). Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ paracellularly.
  • DCT: NCC Na⁺/Cl⁻ (thiazides); Ca²⁺ reabsorption (PTH).
  • Collecting duct: principal cells: ENaC Na⁺ in, K⁺ out (aldosterone; amiloride, spironolactone); aquaporin-2 water reabsorption (ADH); intercalated cells: H⁺/HCO₃⁻ (acid–base).
SecretionH⁺, K⁺, organic acids/bases and drugs (penicillin, methotrexate) in PCT via OAT/OCT transporters; creatinine (small amount).
Excretion = filtration − reabsorption + secretion. Urine output ~1–2 L/day.

los.text: Explain how glomerular filtrate forms and the regulation of GFR
los.html:
Net filtration pressure
  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (~55 mmHg) − Bowman's capsule pressure (~15) − plasma oncotic pressure (~30) ≈ 10 mmHg.
  • GFR = Kf × NFP ≈ 125 mL/min (~180 L/day).
Afferent vs efferent arterioleAfferent constriction ↓ GFR; efferent constriction ↑ GFR (angiotensin II maintains GFR when perfusion falls).
Autoregulation(MAP ~80–180 mmHg keeps GFR steady)
  • Myogenic: ↑ stretch → afferent constriction.
  • Tubuloglomerular feedback: ↑ NaCl at macula densa → adenosine → afferent constriction (and ↓ renin).
NeurohormonalSympathetic (afferent constriction, ↓ GFR in shock), angiotensin II (efferent > afferent constriction), prostaglandins (afferent dilation), ANP (↑ GFR).
Drugs: NSAIDs (block afferent PG dilation) + ACEi/ARB (block efferent constriction) + diuretics ("triple whammy") → AKI, especially when dehydrated.
  • Measurement: inulin clearance (gold standard), creatinine clearance (overestimates slightly due to secretion), eGFR (CKD-EPI equation). Creatinine depends on muscle mass.

los.text: Describe the control of micturition and what the composition of urine should be in health
los.html:
BladderDetrusor (smooth muscle), trigone. Internal sphincter (smooth muscle, bladder neck; males), external sphincter (striated, voluntary; pudendal nerve S2–4).
Storage
  • Sympathetic (hypogastric nerve, T10–L2) → β3 detrusor relaxation + α1 bladder neck contraction
  • Somatic (pudendal) keeps external sphincter closed.
  • Spinal guarding reflex.
Voiding
  • Stretch receptors
  • → pelvic nerve afferents
  • → pontine micturition centre (when socially appropriate, frontal cortex releases inhibition)
  • → parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic S2–4, M3) detrusor contraction + sphincter relaxation.
Capacity ~400–600 mL; first urge ~150–250 mL.
Dysfunction
  • Suprasacral spinal cord lesion → detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia (spastic bladder)
  • Sacral/cauda equina lesion → atonic bladder, retention with overflow
  • Cortical lesion (stroke, dementia) → urge incontinence.
Normal urine
  • 0.8–2 L/day
  • pH ~4.5–8 (typically ~6)
  • Specific gravity 1.005–1.030
  • Osmolality 50–1200 mOsm/kg
  • Contains urea, creatinine, Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, urate.
  • No glucose, significant protein (<150 mg/day), blood, nitrites, leucocytes or bilirubin
  • Trace urobilinogen.

los.text: Describe the fundamental concepts in psychology and sociology relevant to medicine and health
los.html:
Learning theoriesClassical conditioning (Pavlov: anticipatory nausea before chemotherapy), operant conditioning (Skinner: reinforcement/punishment shapes behaviour, e.g. illness behaviours rewarded), social learning (Bandura: modelling, self-efficacy).
Cognition
  • Attention
  • Perception
  • Memory (patients forget ~40–80% of medical information quickly; use chunking, written info, teach-back)
  • Heuristics and biases in clinical reasoning (anchoring, availability).
Development across the lifespanAttachment (Bowlby, Ainsworth: secure vs insecure), Piaget's cognitive stages, Erikson's psychosocial stages; ageing.
Personality and individual differencesBig Five; type A behaviour; locus of control.
Doctor–patient communicationPatient-centred consultation (Calgary–Cambridge), ICE (ideas, concerns, expectations), shared decision-making.
Adherence
  • ~30–50% don't take medicines as prescribed.
  • Intentional (beliefs about necessity vs concerns) vs unintentional (forgetting, complexity).
  • Improve with simpler regimens, explanation and shared decisions.
Social factorsSocial support buffers stress; social class and gender shape illness experience and healthcare use; labelling and stigma.
